claims.text: In single-phase high-entropy alloys, lattice-distortion strengthening is the key mechanism governing hardness and strength.
Atomic-size mismatch induces local strain fields.
Local strain fields caused by atomic-size mismatch impede dislocation motion.
Arc melting followed by homogenization at approximately 1200 °C for 24 hours in an inert atmosphere can produce a single-phase, well-equilibrated HEA microstructure.
Substituting elements having larger differences in atomic radius will enhance lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortions can be observed through XRD peak broadening.
Local lattice distortions and strain fields around dislocations can be observed by TEM.
Local stress fields generated by lattice distortion impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases hardness and yield strength.
HEAs with greater atomic-size mismatch will show increased XRD peak broadening relative to the minimized-mismatch baseline.
HEAs with greater atomic-size mismatch will show more pronounced local strain fields in TEM relative to the minimized-mismatch baseline.
HEAs with greater atomic-size mismatch will exhibit more than a 10% increase in hardness and yield strength relative to the minimized-mismatch baseline.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply to well-homogenized, single-phase HEAs under ambient-temperature, quasi-static loading.
At high temperatures, diffusion-related mechanisms may overshadow lattice-distortion strengthening.
In multiphase HEAs, precipitation strengthening may overshadow lattice-distortion strengthening.
The qualitative relationship between atomic-size mismatch and strengthening is well supported in theory.
The quantitative scaling of hardness and yield strength with measured lattice distortion is uncertain.
Other strengthening mechanisms, including solid-solution and precipitation strengthening, could alter the observed trends if they are not controlled.
